title: Adon Olam
hook: a medieval poem ending in trust: the Lord is with me, I shall not fear

segments.voice: Yesterday, why mourners say the Kaddish, and why it takes ten. Your line was the community answers. Today, a song that starts with the universe and ends at your pillow.

Here's a party trick from Jewish summer camps. Pick almost any tune, a folk song, a pop chorus, a sea shanty, and somebody will fit Adon Olam to it. The poem's lines are so even, so regular, that the words slide onto nearly any melody. So in some synagogues it's sung to a different tune every week, often at the very end of the Shabbat service, kids running up front to sing it. It's light and bouncy. And it's about time before the world began, and about falling asleep.
screen: `ANY TUNE WILL DO.` → `KIDS RUN UP TO SING IT.` → `BEFORE THE WORLD, AND BEDTIME.`

segments.voice: Adon olam means Lord of the world, or Master of the universe. Nobody knows for sure who wrote it. It's sometimes credited to Solomon ibn Gabirol, a Hebrew poet of Muslim Spain, but the evidence is thin. It's medieval, and its even meter resembles the kind Hebrew poets in Spain used. The poem moves like a camera zooming in. It begins before anything existed: Lord of the world, who reigned before any form was made. Without beginning, without end. God, vast and alone. Then, halfway through, the voice turns. He is my God, my living redeemer, the rock in my time of trouble. Suddenly it isn't the universe. It's me. And the last lines come down to the smallest scene there is. Into his hand I entrust my spirit, when I sleep and when I wake. And with my spirit, my body too. The Lord is with me; I shall not fear. Those lines lean on two psalms. In the old Jewish translation, Psalm 31: "Into Thy hand I commit my spirit." And Psalm 118: "The LORD is for me; I will not fear." That's why Adon Olam is also in the bedtime prayers of many prayer books: the one praying hands over their spirit for the night, and trusts it will come back in the morning. A poem about infinity, ending with someone falling asleep without fear.
screen: `LORD OF THE WORLD.` · `BEFORE ANY FORM WAS MADE.` · `THE VOICE TURNS: MY GOD.` · `INTO HIS HAND, WHEN I SLEEP.` · then, large: `I SHALL NOT FEAR.`

segments.voice: Pick a tune that's easy in your mouth, and if you know Adon Olam, sing its last line to it quietly; if not, hum the tune and hold the meaning, I shall not fear. Sing it twice, then let it fade and sit in the quiet after, the way a room does when the service ends.
Adon Olam. Lord of the world. A medieval poem that zooms from eternity to one person falling asleep in trust.
Your line: I shall not fear. Into his hand, when I sleep and when I wake. Six hundred five days now.
